talk.label: 02 / Then just talk
talk.h2: No commands to learn. Just talk.
talk.lede: Say what you want. The agent runs the workflow, shows each draft and asks before it writes. The scenes below are Claude Code; in Codex the same flow is experimental.
talk.s1.name: Decide
talk.s1.p: A decision becomes an ADR with its rejected alternatives. Nothing is written without your yes, and a critic with a fresh context reviews it after.
talk.s1.tty: > We keep sessions in Redis, not in the database.● decision-detector · this is a decision: write it down as an ADR?? Write the ADR? › Yes+ ADR written · review_status: pending● critic · fresh contextrevise — what happens to sessions when Redis restarts?? Apply the fix? › Yes● fixed: persistence on; a lost session asks to log in again✓ review_status: reviewed
talk.s2.name: Plan
talk.s2.p: Gaps are caught while they are still sentences, not bugs.
talk.s2.tty: > Split “checkout with saved cards” into an epic and stories.● epic CHECKOUT · the goal, the scope, 4 stories planned? Write the epic? › Yes+ epics/CHECKOUT/epic.md · review_status: pending● critic revise — no story covers a declined saved card? Add that story to the plan? › Yes● 5 stories, each with acceptance criteria, each written on your yes
talk.s3.name: Build
talk.s3.p: The planner says where the change belongs. The reviewer asks for evidence on every acceptance criterion before the story closes.
talk.s3.tty: > Take the next story in CHECKOUT.● planner · src/billing/cards/ — reuse PaymentGateway● implemented · 4 files · tests pass● reviewer criterion 2 has no evidence: the bank's reason on a declined card● test added · tests/cards.test.ts:58? Close the story? › Yes✓ story done · evidence under each criterion
talk.s4.name: The next session
talk.s4.p: A new session opens with what is in flight. Name a story, and the agent reads its plan and its checklist from the file.

rails.label: 03 / The rails
rails.h2:
Gather context → act → verify.
Over the project, not just the code.
loop.cap: The ProjectStore loop. Decide: a task from you, an ADR, spec or story, an independent critic, your approval. Build: the planner, the implementation, an independent reviewer, done. Each artifact lands in the vault, and the next session sees it.
loop.views: board, link graph and code map regenerate
loop.l.1: You say what you want. The agent opens an artifact before it opens an editor.
loop.l.2: An ADR when something needs deciding, an epic and stories for the work, a spec when the "how" is not obvious. Previewed, and written on your yes.
loop.l.3: A critic with a fresh context, and no stake in the draft, attacks it. Expect "revise".
loop.l.4: You approve the fixes. The artifact is marked reviewed and lands in the backlog.
loop.l.5: An agent picks up a story. The planner reads how earlier epics landed in the code and says where this change belongs.
loop.l.6: Code and tests, following the story's plan.
loop.l.7: A reviewer with a fresh context checks the diff against each acceptance criterion and asks for evidence.
loop.l.8: Done, with evidence under each criterion. The board, the link graph and the code map regenerate.

Project artifacts.

fits.p.10: Decision logs, validators, session-start orientation and independent review each exist elsewhere. What ProjectStore adds is all of them over one linked record.

modes.label: 06 / Solo or a team
modes.h2: One vault. Many sessions, people and agents.
teams.p.12: Two agents or two people in one vault at the same time is normal. Each session knows about the others, and a few simple rules keep them out of each other's way.
teams.h3.1: Everyone sees more than their own part.
teams.p.2: The developer, the tech lead and QA work from the same decisions and criteria. A person without an agent needs only GitHub or a Markdown editor: it is just files.
teams.h3.2: Shared contracts. Separate areas of work.
teams.p.4: In one project, the API, Web and Platform teams run their own epics on top of shared ADRs and specs. A change to a shared contract is discussed in review with the teams that use it. ProjectStore shows which stories depend on it.
teams.p.6: The planner reads the decisions and the code map. The implementer reads the story and the spec. The reviewer reads the diff and the criteria. Each gets the context it needs, not the whole history of someone else's session. Sessions on the same vault warn each other.

method.label: 07 / The method, proof and questions
why.h2.1:
The industry invented this long ago.
Agents made it cheap.
why.p.1: ADRs, reviews, a backlog, acceptance criteria, links from goal to code. Mature engineering teams have worked this way for twenty years. ProjectStore invents none of it.
why.tl.1: RFCs: decisions written down and numbered, then discussed in the open.
why.tl.2: DO-178B: in avionics, every requirement must trace to code and to a test.
why.tl.3: Scrum: the work as a backlog, ordered and visible.
why.tl.4: XP: user stories, and acceptance criteria that say when one is done.
why.tl.5: Kanban for software: a board that shows what is in flight.
why.tl.6: ADRs, Michael Nygard: one short file per architectural decision.
why.tl.now: Coding agents: every step takes minutes. Without the artifacts, every session starts empty.
method.why: The full story, from the industry's history →
method.d.1: The loop step by step, the six agents, and the mechanisms that hold it together instead of discipline.
method.d.2: ADRs, backlogs, acceptance criteria, traceability: decades of practice, and what was always expensive about it.
method.d.3: Many sessions, two agents and a whole team on one vault, and the why reviewed like code.
method.f.1: commands the agent runs for you

questions.p.2: No. A memory plugin remembers what the agent said. ProjectStore records what the project decided, as reviewed documents with a status and a date. New work then goes through those documents. The difference shows when you switch agents, machines or teammates: memory belongs to an agent, a user or a machine, and even memory kept in git is the agent's own notes; the vault is the project's record — approved, reviewed, with a status — and travels through git.
questions.p.4: No. The vault is an ordinary folder of Markdown files. Open it in an editor, browse it on GitHub, or use Obsidian if you like its graph and board. Without the plugin, the files stay just as readable.
questions.summary.4: Does it ever write without asking?
questions.p.5: No. Every new file or edit is shown to you first, with its path and full text. Then it waits for Yes, Edit before saving, or No. The helpers that watch the conversation only suggest a command. The only agent that can write, the clerk, runs after your Yes and saves exactly what you approved.
questions.summary.10: What stays if I remove it?
questions.p.11: Your vault, untouched: it is plain Markdown in its own git repository. The project's binding and the team's agent models stay too, so setting it up again finds them. Codex's plugin is registered for every project on the machine, so removing it there is a step of its own. How to remove it

hero.post.label: The problem
how.meta.title: How ProjectStore works — the loop, the agents, the guards
how.h1: A loop with an independent check in it.
how.lead: Agents write code fast, and they re-decide settled questions just as fast: every fresh session arrives empty. The fix is not a smarter agent. It is gather context → act → verify, run over the project and not only over the code.
how.loop.label: The loop
how.loop.h2: Eight steps. Two of them are checks by an agent that did not write the draft.
how.agents.label: The agents
agents.h2.2: All but one may only read.
agents.p.1: The advisors check, plan and tidy up, and change nothing. One clerk saves only what you approved, after your Yes.
agents.td.1: After an ADR, spec, epic, story or design is written or changed
agents.td.2: Looks for weak spots, checks every claim against the source and asks how the plan could fail. No flattery.
agents.td.4: Before work on a story starts (story plan)
agents.td.5: Looks at where earlier epics live in the code. Says where the change belongs, what to reuse, what to watch out for and in what order to work.
agents.td.7: After code, before commit or story close
agents.td.8: Asks for proof on every acceptance criterion, including the spec's. Then checks correctness, regressions and tests.
agents.td.10: From time to time, before releases, after the vault grows fast
agents.td.11: Finds what no rule can catch: research notes that contradict an accepted ADR, duplicates, missing links, files ready to archive.
agents.td.13: Once, after binding an existing codebase
agents.td.14: Finds decisions nobody wrote down, in the code, config files and git history. Suggests ADRs for them, with evidence.
agents.td.16: Only inside a command flow, only after your Yes
agents.td.17: Saves exactly what you approved, nothing more. Then rebuilds the board and runs the checks. Writes nothing of its own and asks nothing.
agents.p.10: The default models are Claude Code's. In Codex each role is a skill of the same name that asks Codex to start the role, such as $projectstore-critic for the critic; it uses the session's model unless you set one.
how.mech.label: The guards
how.mech.h2: Mechanisms hold it together, not discipline.
how.m.1.p: An agent that starts editing code with no story open is reminded to open one. A feature-sized change starts in the vault.
how.m.2.p: An artifact that needs review carries review_status: pending until a critic pass is applied. "Not yet reviewed" is a state the tools can read, not something someone must remember.
how.m.3.h: A doctor with no AI in it
how.m.3.p: doctor checks the vault's mechanical consistency deterministically. In CI it runs with no agent and no tokens.
how.m.4.p: graph.md holds every artifact's links in both directions; code-map.md says where each epic's code lives. Before an architectural choice, the agent is pointed at the ADR index first.
how.m.5.p: In Claude Code, after a /compact you run, the session starts with the vault's orientation again, and with the vault files the conversation touched before it.
how.m.6.p: A session that starts while another one works on the same vault opens with a multi-session warning: search before creating anything new.
how.ev.label: Done means proven
how.ev.h2: A story closes with evidence under each criterion.
how.story: --- type: story epic: "CHECKOUT" title: "Saved cards are listed at checkout" status: done code_refs: ["src/billing/cards/", "tests/cards.test.ts"] closed_at: "2026-07-14T16:02:11Z" --- ## Acceptance Criteria - [x] Saved cards are listed first — evidence: tests/cards.test.ts:21 - [x] A declined card shows the bank's reason — evidence: tests/cards.test.ts:58 - [x] No card number reaches the logs — evidence: tests/cards.test.ts:73
how.ev.p.1: The planner said where the change belongs before the code, and the plan went into the story on your yes; the reviewer checked the diff against each criterion after it. Each line of proof is a test, a command that ran, or a line of code.
how.ev.p.2: Any agent can read this record, with or without the plugin: through the CLI, which answers with JSON and needs no tokens, or through the MCP server's 8 read-only tools.
how.fine.label: Fine print
how.fine.1: Running the loop costs tokens: the drafts, the critic and the reviewer run on the model you already pay for. The README measures it.
how.fine.2: The critic and the reviewer are separate agents with a fresh context in Claude Code. In Codex the roles are skills, and that path is experimental.
how.fine.3: ProjectStore is shared project context and a way of working. It is not an agent orchestrator: launching agents is your harness's job.
how.meta.description: The ProjectStore loop step by step: an artifact before code, an independent critic, a planner that knows where earlier work landed, a reviewer that asks for evidence. Six agents, five of them read-only. Claude Code, and Codex (experimental).
why.meta.title: Why ProjectStore works — old engineering practice, made cheap by agents
why.tl.label: Where each piece comes from
why.art.label: What the artifacts do
why.art.h2: One project, many hands. The same ground for all of them.
why.art.p.1: An ADR says what was decided and what was rejected. A spec says how it must work. An epic and its stories say what is being built and when each part is done. The board shows what is in flight.
why.art.p.2: With them, an engineer who joins tomorrow, a reviewer from another team and an agent in a fresh session all start from what the first person knew. That is why teams that build large systems have kept these documents for decades.
why.cost.label: The expensive part
why.p.4: The process was always valuable. What was expensive was people running every step of it.
why.p.3: The process works. Its documents are the most valuable thing a company keeps after a project: why the system is built this way, what counted as done, where each feature lives in the code. But when people run it by hand, it is slow. An ADR takes an afternoon to write and a week to get reviewed. Documents fall behind the code. The board stops matching reality. So teams cut corners, and "agile" becomes an excuse to write nothing down.
why.miss: Where the artifacts are missing, it looks the same with people and with agents: settled questions come back, nobody can say why the code is the way it is, and every newcomer starts by guessing.
why.p.5: Agents are the opposite. Writing an ADR, splitting an epic into stories or checking a diff against criteria takes an agent minutes, not days. What an agent lacks is what people get for free: memory between sessions, context shared with colleagues, the link from a goal to the code. Every new session starts empty and decides again what was already settled.
why.p.6: ProjectStore puts the two together. Agent speed makes the old process cheap for the first time. Its documents, kept in files beside the code, give agents what they never had: the project's context, linked up to the goals and down to the code. A second agent that did not write the draft reviews each step, by rule. Speed gets a memory, and memory gets a check.
why.st.label: Six stages
why.st.h2: Six stages, by hand and in ProjectStore.
why.div.6: ADR, Michael Nygard, 2011. Before that, architecture boards and design review.
why.div.7: An afternoon to write, a week in the review queue. The rejected alternatives stay in someone's head.
why.div.8: The agent drafts it in a minute. A separate critic looks for weak spots. You approve. The result is a dated file that also records what was rejected.
why.div.10: Spec, design doc, RFC. RFCs have been numbered since 1969; design docs are the norm in large companies.
why.div.11: Takes a week to write and is stale by release. Nobody checks that the code still matches it.
why.div.12: A spec lists the expected behaviour as numbered rules. Its checks apply to every story it covers. A story cannot close while its spec is still a draft.
why.div.14: Product backlog from Scrum, 1995. User stories from XP, 1999. Kanban for software, 2007.
why.div.15: Grooming meetings. The board drifts from reality within a week because it is maintained by hand.
why.div.16: Each story file holds its own status. The board, indexes and link map are built from those files. If they drift, one command rebuilds them.
why.div.18: Technical design, impact analysis. The tech lead looks at where this lands in the existing code.
why.div.19: Knowledge of how earlier features landed in the code exists only in the tech lead's head. They are on holiday.
why.div.20: The planner looks at where earlier epics landed in the code. It says where the change belongs and what to reuse. The plan goes into the story.
why.div.22: Acceptance criteria, Definition of Done. XP and Scrum, early 2000s.
why.div.23: A QA cycle at the end of the sprint. "Done" by declaration; criteria spot-checked.
why.div.24: The reviewer checks the diff against every criterion and asks for proof: a test, a command that was run, a line of code. No proof, no close.
why.div.26: Requirements traceability. Mandatory in avionics since DO-178B (1992) and in medical software.
why.div.27: An Excel matrix "requirement → code → test" that nobody updates after the second release.
why.div.28: Every story links up to its epic, ADRs and specs, and down to its code. Proof sits under each acceptance criterion. The link map and the code map are generated, so nobody maintains them by hand.
why.ch.label: The chain
why.h3.1: The links an agent gets for free: from goal to proof
why.span.9: CHECKOUT · why we are doing this
why.span.12: the decision and the rejected options
why.span.21: src/billing/cards/ · where earlier epics already live
why.p.7: The links live in the header of each file, and the proof is a line under each acceptance criterion. The agent fills all of it in as it works. The link map shows what each document connects to. The code map shows where each epic's code lives. A new session, a new model or a new colleague starts from this chain, not from nothing.
why.meta.description: ADRs, specs, backlogs, acceptance criteria and traceability are decades old. Running them by hand was the expensive part. Agents make each step take minutes; the artifacts give agents the memory they lack.
why.aria-label.2: Industry practices, executed by humans and by ProjectStore
vault.meta.title: One vault, many people — ProjectStore for sessions, teams and agents
vault.h1: Many sessions. Many people. One vault.
teams.p.1: The context belongs to the team, not to one developer's chat. ADRs and specs go through pull requests, like code. What gets reviewed is the reasoning.
vault.modes.label: Four ways to work
teams.li.1: No silent overwrites. Before saving a new file, ProjectStore checks that it does not exist yet. Two sessions on the same topic get a clash, not two copies.
teams.li.2: Each status line shows its own work. 2–6 sessions side by side each see exactly their own epic and story.
teams.li.3: Session names are offered, not imposed. Once a session settles on one piece of work, it suggests a name for it. Rarely: at most twice a session, 12 offers across nine recorded sessions.
vault.tty: developer A has worked on CHECKOUT since 13:35. you open a second session: ⚠ Multi-session warning — 1 other projectstore session active. Run /projectstore:search <topic> before creating new artifacts. later, once your work settles on “Saved cards are listed at checkout”: projectstore: this session looks like "checkout-saved-cards-are-listed-at-checkout" → /rename checkout-saved-cards-are-listed-at-checkout
teams.p.3: The context is available to the whole team, not only to the owner of the chat.
teams.p.5: Who owns which artifacts and who signs off on contracts is the team's call.
teams.p.7: Launching agents and handing work between them is the job of your harness or orchestrator.
teams.span.8: An example of organizing the work, not live orchestration
teams.span.24: the vault in its own repository
teams.span.23: What it looks like in git
teams.title.1: Developers with their own agents bind to one vault in its own git repository. ADRs and specs are reviewed as pull requests. A teammate without an agent reviews on GitHub or in Obsidian.
teams.text.11: its own git repo · plain markdown
teams.figcaption.1: Put the vault in its own repository. Everyone installs ProjectStore, binds to the same vault and saves changes only after approval. A teammate without an agent reviews on GitHub or in Obsidian.
vault.setup.label: Setup
teams.h3.4: A team setup, step by step
teams.p.8: One repository of project documents per project, not per person. It sits next to the code repository.
vault.p.9: Each person clones the vault repository, then runs npx projectstore setup in their own copy of the code and names that clone as the vault. The binding stays on that machine and is not committed.
teams.h4.3: A branch and a pull request
teams.p.10: A person reviews each decision before it is accepted. The critic checks it before the pull request; your team reviews it inside.
teams.p.11: npx projectstore doctor --json runs in CI with no agent and no tokens. It fails the step when it finds problems. reconcile --write can rebuild the board there too.
vault.codex: Claude Code and Codex can work one project side by side: they share the binding, and each keeps its own agent models and session state.
vault.meta.description: Several sessions, a whole team and several agents on one ProjectStore vault: the rules that keep them apart, the vault in its own git repository, ADRs and specs reviewed as pull requests, and a team setup in four steps.
